records.briefTitle: The Study of Nasal Insulin in the Fight Against Forgetfulness (SNIFF)
records.officialTitle: Therapeutic Effects of Intranasally-Administered Insulin in Adults With Amnestic Mild Cognitive Impairment (aMCI) or Mild Alzheimer's Disease (AD)
records.briefSummary:
An urgent need exists to find effective treatments for Alzheimer's disease (AD) that can arrest or reverse the disease at its earliest stages. The emotional and financial burden of AD to patients, family members, and society is enormous, and is predicted to grow exponentially as the median population age increases. Current FDA-approved therapies are modestly effective at best. This study will examine a novel therapeutic approach using intranasal insulin (INI) that has shown promise in short-term clinical trials. If successful, information gained from the study has the potential to move INI forward rapidly as a therapy for AD. The study will also provide evidence for the mechanisms through which INI may produce benefits by examining key cerebral spinal fluid (CSF) biomarkers and hippocampal/entorhinal atrophy. These results will have considerable clinical and scientific significance, and provide therapeutically-relevant knowledge about insulin's effects on AD pathophysiology. Growing evidence has shown that insulin carries out multiple functions in the brain, and that insulin dysregulation may contribute to AD pathogenesis.

This study will examine the effects of intranasally-administered insulin on cognition, entorhinal cortex and hippocampal atrophy, and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) biomarkers in amnestic mild cognitive impairment (aMCI) or mild AD. It is hypothesized that after 12 months of treatment with INI compared to placebo, subjects will improve performance on a global measure of cognition, on a memory composite and on daily function. In addition to the examination of CSF biomarkers and hippocampal and entorhinal atrophy, the study aims to examine whether baseline AD biomarker profile, gender, or Apolipoprotein epsilon 4 (APOE-ε4) allele carriage predict treatment response.

In this study, 240 people with aMCI or AD will be given either INI or placebo for 12 months, following an open-label period of 6 months where all participants will be given active drug. The study uses insulin as a therapeutic agent and intranasal administration focusing on nose to brain transport as a mode of delivery.
primaryOutcomes: Change in Global Measure of Cognition as Measured by the Alzheimer's Disease Assessment Scale-Cognitive 12 (ADAS-Cog12)

records.briefTitle: RE-RITE: Real-world Evaluation of Response, Implementation and Toxicity of Elranatamab
records.officialTitle: RE-RITE: Real-world Evaluation of Response, Implementation and Toxicity of Elranatamab
records.organization: The Royal Wolverhampton Hospitals NHS Trust
records.leadSponsor: The Royal Wolverhampton Hospitals NHS Trust
records.briefSummary:
Elranatamab is an effective BCMA-targeting bispecific antibody for relapsed/refractory multiple myeloma (RRMM). However, implementation in routine practice remains challenging due to monitoring requirements during step-up dosing for cytokine release syndrome (CRS) and immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS), together with the long-term burden of infection prevention and immunoglobulin replacement. Delivery models across the NHS vary considerably, including inpatient, ambulatory, outpatient, and virtual ward step-up dosing approaches. Supportive-care practice also evolved following NHS commissioning of primary immunoglobulin replacement for selected patients with hypogammaglobulinaemia.

This study will evaluate real-world implementation of elranatamab across the NHS to identify approaches to safe, scalable, and equitable delivery. Primary objectives are to evaluate acute delivery pathways for CRS/ICANS management during step-up dosing and long-term infection management, including immunoglobulin replacement. Secondary objectives include assessment of healthcare resource utilisation, treatment delivery patterns, infection outcomes, and clinical outcomes across diverse healthcare and socioeconomic settings.

The study population will be RRMM patients receiving elranatamab through NHS funding or compassionate access programmes from 01/01/2024 till 31/12/2026. Patients treated within clinical trials will be excluded.

This national multicentre retrospective observational study will utilise the UKCHART research network, with 20 participating tertiary and district general hospitals. Variation in delivery pathways, toxicity management strategies, and supportive-care practices, together with changes in NHS immunoglobulin replacement policy, has created a natural experiment in elranatamab implementation. Approximately 400 patients are anticipated. There will be two retrospective data collection sweeps. The first will capture baseline characteristics, treatment history, delivery pathways, toxicity management, infection prevention strategies, healthcare resource utilisation, and early outcomes. The second, conducted around 12 months later, will provide longer-term follow-up including infection outcomes, immunoglobulin replacement utilisation, treatment patterns, subsequent therapies, and cumulative resource utilisation.

Analyses will evaluate delivery models, CRS/ICANS management strategies, serious infections requiring hospitalisation, intensive care admission or death, immunoglobulin replacement utilisation, hospital admissions, bed-day utilisation, and variation across healthcare settings and socioeconomic groups.

This study will generate one of the largest national real-world datasets on elranatamab implementation. Findings will inform optimisation of monitoring strategies and supportive-care delivery including infection prevention, to guide evidence-based NHS delivery models for elranatamab and other T-cell redirecting therapies.
records.detailedDescription:
Elranatamab, a BCMA-targeting bispecific antibody, has emerged as an important treatment option in relapsed/refractory multiple myeloma, with clinically meaningful efficacy in patients with multiple prior lines of therapy. However, its clinical use is associated with a distinct toxicity profile, including cytokine release syndrome (CRS), immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS), and an increased risk of infection. As a result, its implementation requires careful operational planning, particularly during step-up dosing and early-cycle monitoring.

Early clinical trial protocols were heavily influenced by CAR-T cell therapy pathways, with inpatient admission frequently used during step-up dosing to mitigate acute toxicity risk. While this approach prioritises safety, it places substantial demands on inpatient capacity and may not be feasible across all treatment centres. This creates potential inequities in access, particularly in hospitals with limited inpatient oncology infrastructure. In response, delivery models in routine clinical practice have evolved rapidly and now vary substantially, ranging from inpatient initiation to ambulatory day-case pathways and, increasingly, outpatient or hybrid virtual ward-based models. These differences largely reflect local infrastructure, service configuration, and institutional risk tolerance rather than a standardised, evidence-based framework.

Although uptake of elranatamab in clinical practice is increasing, there remains limited high-quality real-world evidence defining the optimal intensity of monitoring and care delivery required to ensure safe and efficient administration. In particular, uncertainty remains regarding the minimum level of monitoring that can be safely implemented without increasing clinically meaningful adverse outcomes, including severe CRS, unplanned hospitalisation, or early treatment discontinuation. This evidence gap has important implications for healthcare capacity and scalability, as more intensive inpatient-based approaches may substantially increase bed utilisation and limit equitable access within resource-constrained systems.

In parallel, approaches to infection prevention and immunoglobulin replacement therapy have evolved during the implementation of elranatamab in routine clinical practice. National practice has shifted from predominantly secondary immunoglobulin replacement strategies towards primary prophylaxis in selected patient groups, with current commissioning supporting immunoglobulin replacement in patients with IgG levels below 4 g/L, even in the absence of a significant infection history. This has resulted in routine, often indefinite immunoglobulin replacement during bispecific antibody therapy. While potentially reducing infection risk, this strategy introduces significant cost and treatment burden, effectively constituting dual long-term therapy with both a bispecific antibody and immunoglobulin replacement. Delivery approaches, including intravenous and subcutaneous administration, may also vary between centres, further contributing to heterogeneity in practice.

The clinical and economic impact of these evolving infection prevention strategies remains poorly defined, particularly in the context of sustained B-cell depletion and infection risk associated with BCMA-directed therapies. This represents an important evidence gap with respect to both patient outcomes and healthcare resource utilisation.

There is substantial variation in elranatamab delivery across routine clinical practice, encompassing tertiary and district general hospitals, differing models of ambulatory care provision, and emerging use of virtual ward infrastructure. This heterogeneity, combined with recent changes in immunoglobulin replacement policy, creates a natural experiment in which real-world implementation strategies and their consequences can be systematically evaluated at scale within a single healthcare system.

Taken together, there is a clear need for a national real-world evaluation to define evidence-based pathways for the safe, efficient, and equitable delivery of elranatamab in routine clinical practice. Specifically, there is a need to determine how different delivery models influence safety outcomes, healthcare resource utilisation, infection burden, and treatment continuity, and how evolving supportive care strategies, including immunoglobulin replacement, modify these outcomes. Addressing these gaps is essential to inform scalable implementation across diverse clinical settings while maintaining patient safety and ensuring equitable access to treatment.

The study population will be RRMM patients receiving elranatamab through NHS funding or compassionate access programmes from 01/01/2024 till 31/12/2026. Patients treated within clinical trials will be excluded.

It will be an Ambispective study with Retrospective and Prospective follow up.
primaryOutcomes: Incidence of early severe treatment-related toxicity during step-up dosing
Incidence of serious infection during treatment

records.briefTitle: Novel, Individualized Brain Stimulation, Network-based Approaches to Improve Cognition
records.officialTitle: Novel, Individualized Brain Stimulation, Network-based Approaches to Improve Cognition in Healthy Seniors and Patients With MCI
records.briefSummary: Impaired working memory (WM) plays a crucial role in normal aging, in mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and cognitive decline associated with dementia, such as Alzheimer's disease (AD). The aging-related differences in WM are hypothesized to be based on various neurobiological origins, for example alterations in the dynamic interplay between the large-scale brain networks have proven an important role. Recent studies have shown that non-invasive brain stimulation (NIBS) methods can modulate neuronal activity, plasticity and large-scale brain network interactions. The investigators hypothesize that multifocal NIBS can improve WM. By successive and concurrent stimulation of multiple brain regions of the WM network by transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) and/or repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) the investigators will study dynamic interactions between distinct cortico-cortical and subcortico-cortical brain areas. By leveraging multimodal systems neuroscience information during multifocal stimulation, the investigators expect to acquire better mechanistic understand through which NIBS acts on the brain and improves cognitive functions, such as WM.
records.detailedDescription:
Mild cognitive impairment (MCI) describes an intermediate stage from normal cognitive functioning to dementia, and identifies a spectrum of diseases that includes impairment in both memory and non-memory cognitive domains. A deficient working memory (WM) plays a crucial role in normal aging, MCI, and cognitive decline associated with dementia, such as Alzheimer's disease (AD). WM refers to the on-line temporary storage and manipulation of information to be employed in ongoing processing, and is central to the execution of a variety of daily functions. The loss of WM efficiency related to either aging or neurodegenerative process is hypothesized to have various neurobiological roots, among which altered functioning of the fronto-parietal networks play an important role. The processing, exchange, and storing of information rely on intra- and interregional connectivity that allow neuronal populations to synchronize their firing. Based on this, intra- and cross frequency oscillatory interactions have been demonstrated as core basis for working memory processes, besides other cognitive functions. Any impairment preventing the adaptation and synchronization of the oscillatory activities within this network will inevitably lead to temporary or permanent loss of function.

In this project, based on the mentioned pathophysiological concepts, the investigators will develop and test novel, individualized, multifocal, physiology-inspired non-invasive brain stimulation (NIBS) approaches aimed at enhancing interregional processing in memory-related fronto-parieto-cerebello networks with consecutive behavioral modulation of WM processes impacting on daily life activities in aged healthy volunteers (HV) and MCI patients.

The investigators approach these aims in a step-wise manner: (1) The investigators will explore entrainment of oscillatory activity in the fronto-parietal network with transcranial alternative current stimulation (tACS) at frequencies relevant to memory encoding (theta) to boost WM in healthy seniors. (2) Then, the investigators will explore cross-frequency entrainment of interregional oscillatory interactions in the frontal and parietal target network with bifocal tACS to boost WM in healthy seniors. (3) Based on the current knowledge about the extensive involvement of the cerebellum in cognitive processes by its modulatory effects onto the fronto-parietal networks crucial for cognition, the investigators will leverage our experience in non-invasive modulation of the cerebellar outputs by means of repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS). rTMS over the cerebellum will be applied just before cortical entrainment to further enhance its physiological and behavioral effects. (4) Finally, the investigators will select the most effective approach from the previous work-packages to be applied in MCI patients and quantify the behavioral benefits. Besides the behavioral effects, the investigators will apply multimodal systems neuroscience approaches by means of neuroimaging (structural and functional magnetic resonance imaging; s/fMRI) and electrophysiological (Electroencephalography - EEG, transcranial magnetic stimulation - TMS) methods to determine the underlying network mechanisms and patterns of intrinsic connectivity changes. As there is significant spatial heterogeneity in fronto-parietal peak activity in healthy seniors and patients, stimulation targets will be individually defined based on fMRI. By leveraging the mechanistic aspects derived from individualized multifocal stimulation, the investigators expect to better understand the mechanisms through which NIBS techniques act on the brain and improve cognitive functions. The investigators will also test and quantify within a virtual reality (VR) task how well the intervention-driven cognitive improvement translates into daily life.
primaryOutcomes: Working memory performance
